segments.text: C³-DRIVE Net for Context-Aware Clinically-Grounded Automated Detection, Segmentation, and Severity Grading of Dental Caries in Radiographic Images Abstract- Dental caries is the most prevalent of all long-standing oral diseases globally. The early detection and proper evaluation of lesion severity are particularly important for determining the optimal preventive or therapeutic intervention. It is worth mentioning that dental X-rays interpretation significantly depend on the dentist experience, and may differ across clinicians, particularly when diagnosing early or mild carious lesions. Many existing deep learning algorithms are designed for only one task (e.g., caries detection and segmentation) and process lesions as isolated objects. For all of this, they are unable to easily show us how caries forms slowly or how it relates to the anatomy of our teeth. To alleviate these problems, in this paper we propose the C³-DRIVE Net (Context-aware, Clinically-grounded, Continual Dental Radiographic Intelligence for Visual Explanation), an integration learning framework to simultaneously carry out caries detection, lesion segmentation and their severity grading based on dental X-ray images. The proposed model leverages knowledge in the form of tooth-aware anatomical analysis along with radiographic gradient variations to detect patterns of mineral loss associated with both early and advanced caries. The use of a common multi-task encoder enables the model to learn all tasks across one another, removing error accumulation that is typical in cascaded systems. Radiographic depth of caries and the structural relationship of enamel, dentin, and pulp are employed to score the severity in a manner consistent with clinical grading systems. The experimental results on annotated dental x-ray datasets achieve a detection accuracy of 97.8%, a segmentation Dice score of 91.2% and a severity grading accuracy of 95.6%. Moreover, the proposed approach also enhances 22% early caries detection sensitivity than current deep leaning based methods. These findings confirm that the C³-DRIVE Net is an accurate, interpretable and clinically useful solution for chairside dental diagnosis. Keywords-Dental caries detection, Dental X-ray analysis, Multi-task deep learning, Severity grading, Clinical decision support, Explainable AI. I Introduction​ Dental caries is still one of the most prevalent chronic oral diseases worldwide that occurs throughout all age groups and presents a significant public health challenge [1][2][3]. Radiographic exposures, particularly bitewing and panoramic films are important in the early recognition and follow-up of lesions located on non-visible proximal surfaces and sub-surface areas [4][5]. However, diagnosing dental caries
segments.label: human

segments.text: from radiographs is inherently difficult because low-contrast discriminations exist between sound tissue and mineral loss [6][7], as well as overlapping anatomical structures and differences in image acquisition including angle [8][9]. Demineralization of enamel at an early stage is characteristically radiolucent in appearance and may be so subtle that it is difficult for even experienced clinicians to detect [10][11]. These difficulties lead to diagnostic uncertainty, delayed intervention, and high levels of inter- and intra-observer variability in day-to-day clinical practice. There are promising studies on automated dental caries analysis under development with the recent progress of deep learning [12], however, they mainly addressed either detection or segmentation alone [13][14]. Although some previous methods may have better accuracy for identifying different regions, these studies were based on convolutional neural network–based models that generally use an object or pixel-wise method and are not able to sufficiently model the anatomical context of teeth while lesion development is progressive [15][16]. Furthermore, many techniques are based on cascaded pipelines with detection outputs as inputs of subsequent segmentation or classification stages, which leads to error accumulation and decrease in robustness. Crucially, severity grading—a key aspect for clinical management—is frequently formulated as a crude classification task which is not directly mapped with well-known radiographic criteria, e.g. enamel–dentin–pulp relationships and depth-based lesion progression [17][18]. However, despite the expanding literature, there are three important gaps that have been inadequately filled [19]. First, none of the existing works provide a unifying framework that can jointly detect caries and segment lesions with high precision as well as grade their severity in line with clinical references within an end-to-end architecture [20][21]. Secondly, current models ignore tooth-aware anatomical inferences and radiographic gradient changes exhibited by the mineral densities including early caries [22]. Third, although many deep learning systems are designed as black boxes, they lack explainability and clinical trust to facilitate their application on the real-world chairside [23]. Such restrictions limit the translational potential of existing techniques and call for context-sensitive, explainable, and clinically-grounded diagnostic mechanisms. To tackle these problems, this work defines automated dental caries analysis as a unified multi-task learning problem which learns detection [24], segmentation and severity reasoning jointly from radiographic images. Here we present C³-DRIVE Net, a context aware and clinically informed deep learning architecture, which aims to capture anatomical structure, radiographic intensity disruptions [25][26], and lesion progression signatures in a shared representation space. By combining a tooth-aware anatomical decomposition with radiograph gradient modeling and clinically motivated lesion severity indices, our framework is tailored towards mitigating diagnostic variation, increasing
segments.label: human

segments.text: sensitivity to early-stage lesions and producing interpretable outputs in a manner consistent with existing clinical practice [27]. This integrated formulation is designed to be a compromise of algorithmic performance and practical clinical utility. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: ●​ An end-to-end multitask deep learning model to detect caries, segment lesions, and grade their severity avoiding the error-prone cascaded approach. ●​ A radiographically based severity ranking system that includes depth indices and enamel–dentin–pulp relationships as they relate to clinical parameters is described, compatible with established diagnostic guidelines. ●​ A context-sensitive model that utilises tooth-level anatomic decomposition and radiation gradient disruption analysis to enhance sensitivity for, and interpretability of, early diagnosed caries. 1.1 Objectives of the Study​ The purpose of this study is to investigate: ●​ To design an integrated deep learning model for effecting simultaneous optimization of detection, segmentation and severity grading of dental caries in radiographic images. ●​ To provide anatomic and radiographic context for learning, improve early lesion detection rates and minimize diagnostic confusion. ●​ To develop a clinically applicative severity grading system that facilitates reproducible decision-making in an everyday dental diagnostic laboratory. This paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work and identifies existing research gaps. Section III presents the proposed C³-DRIVE Net framework, followed by Section IV describing the experimental setup, Section V discussing results and analysis, and Section VI concluding the paper with limitations and future directions. II Literature Review​ Panyarak et al. (2023) attempted to investigate whether deep learning was compatible for classifying dental caries severity on the bitewing X-ray in accordance with the ICCMS™ scoring system. They trained several ResNet models and indicated that the best model performed reasonably well for a 4-level severity classification but not so well for detailed, 7-level ICCMS™ grading, particularly in detecting early enamel caries. This indicated that image-level classification may be inadequate for a more nuanced grading of severity in complexity without tooth anatomy features [1]. Chen et al. (2023) presented a two-stage system for severity classification of caries in panoramic X-rays. They firstly separated teeth extracted by a modified U-Net with ASPP and boundary loss. They then utilized a rule-based analysis to establish caries extent. This would allow for easier identification of tissue boundaries and interpretation by clinicians. However, since it utilized a sequential approach the errors
segments.label: human

segments.text: in initial phases might impede later steps and the technique can be hard to scale [2]. In another study, Chen et al. (2023) proposed a framework to achieve the identification of periodontitis and dental caries on periapical X-rays. The model leveraged YOLOv7 to detect teeth and EfficientNet for disease classification. Despite high performance, the system still considered dental decay in yes/no terms only (in or out of caries), without lesion area localisation and severity assessment [3]. A hybrid approach proposed by Vimalarani and Ramachandraiah (2022) combined conventional image preprocessing techniques, handcrafted descriptors, and a LeNet architecture-based deep classifier for caries detection in bitewing radiographs. The approach achieved good accuracy, however it heavily relied on manual feature generation and heuristic-based segmentation that restricts its use across varied X-ray qualities and clinical environments [4]. Esmaeilyfard et al. (2024) proposed deep learning for caries detection and classification with CBCT volume. Their multiple input CNN also demonstrated a good performance for detection of the caries presence and assessment of the depth and location of the lesion. But the study was targeted at 3D CBCT data which is not directly applicable to routine screening by 2D dental radiography [5]. Estai et al. (2022) introduced a Siamese-CNN based two-staged architecture for proximal caries detection in bitewing radiographs. Regions of interest were extracted using Faster R-CNN, and then they were classified by Inception-ResNet-v2. While it maintains reasonable precision and recall rates for object detections, the cascaded structure raised complexity and made the model more error sensitive [6]. Panyarak et al. (2023) similarly analyzed YOLOv3 with varied IoU thresholds for ICCMS™-based caries detection. Although adequately accurate in those with relatively advanced lesions, the model was unable to detect superficial enamel caries consistently thus indicating the inferiority of object-detection-based approaches in recognizing subtle radiographic changes [7]. Ahmed et al. (2023) used semantic segmentation for caries detection of bitewing X-ray images with an extension of KAU classification. However, segmentation accuracy for early enamel and dentin caries were low, which indicated that it is challenging to mark the early lesions accurately [8]. Albano et al. (2024) performed a systematic study of AI based caries detection strategies from various dental imaging modalities. This review found that there were wide differences in datasets, evaluation metrics, and performance outcomes generated by published studies and the lack of standardization and scarce variety of data are still considerable challenges to clinical use [9]. Bayrakdar et al. (2022) utilized CNN to automatically detect caries with the combined use of U-Net for the important task of lesion segmentation in BW-Xray images. Their findings indicated that AI systems could outperform junior dentists. Detection and segmentation were nonetheless processed separately from each other, with no caries severity grading addressed in the work [10]. Kunt et al. (2023)
segments.label: human

segments.text: introduced a large and highly annotated bitewing radiograph dataset and tested numerous object-detection models, including YOLO, Faster R-CNN. These models achieved a level of accuracy similar to that of experienced dentists. However, sensitivity was quite reduced for small and incipient caries, demonstrating how difficult remains the early detection of these lesions [11]. Park et al. (2022) compared caries detection by using intraoral photograph images and x-ray. By partitioning tooth surfaces prior to classification, they demonstrated the benefit of anatomic information for detection. Nevertheless, the study did not investigate radiographic imaging or caries severity evaluation [12]. Yoon et al. (2024) also proposed a cascade R-CNN model that leveraged integrated tooth number recognition and caries detection for full intraoral images. The system showed good localization and counting performance, but allowed only detection, not determining depth or severity of lesion for caries analysis [13]. Ayhan et al. (2025) applied YOLO-based models for caries detection under the fixed dental prosthesis on panoramic radiographs. Their two-stage method increased accuracy in challenging clinical contexts but was still focused on object-level detection as opposed to lesion segmentation or severity grading [14]. Bui et al. (2022) presented an ensemble learning framework that integrated deep features and machine-learning classifiers for caries detection in panoramic X-rays. While the system performed with high accuracy, this majority-voting strategy had limited interpretability and did not result in severity values that were clinically informative [15]. Szabó et al. (2024) assessed an AI-based diagnostic system by measuring the degree of agreement between dentists and AI regarding the radiographs of intraoral. They established that AI can provide valuable assistance to clinical diagnosis, but the sensitivity was moderate, particularly for initial caries which calls for better frame of reference [16]. Zhu et al. (2023) introduced CariesNet, a U-shaped network with axial attention for the segmentation of caries at different stages in panoramic radiography. The model obtained high Dice coefficients for superficial, intermediate and deep lesions. Nevertheless, the interpretation for intensity was implied and not explicitly related to levels based on classic clinical grading scales [17]. Sehgal et al. (2025) constructed a fuzzy logic-based scheme to categorize the severity of caries on the basis of handcrafted features computed upon region of interest (ROI) segmented from the X-ray images. Although we achieved high accuracy, our rule-based methodology is not as scalable and adaptive as the deep learning methods in today’s practices [18]. 2.1 Key Insight from Literature The existing studies show good performance in detection, segmentation or classification dental caries. However, most of them treat these tasks separately or are organized in a cascaded way and also do not have clinically informed severity modeling for early stage lesions. It is these challenges that drive the necessity for a
segments.label: human

segments.text: unified, context-aware and clinically-driven multi-task approach as in our proposed C³-DRIVE Net. III Proposed C³-DRIVE Net Framework The proposed C³-DRIVE Net is a holistic multitasking architecture that achieves both dental caries detection 19 and lesion segmentation, along with clinically interpretable severity grading, in a single joint end-to-end framework [21]. The general model architecture is based on encoder–decoder–multi-head, wherein shared encoder learns hierarchical radiographic representations that describe intensity gradients, anatomical structures and texture variations potentially correlated with mineral loss. This encoder is linked to a dual-decoder branch: a spatial decoder which maintains high-resolution feature maps for accurate lesion segmentation and semantic decoder consolidating global context information for robust caries detection [22]. Three task-specific heads are used on top of the shared representation: (i) a detection head that indicates locations of various regions at tooth level, (ii) a segmentation head delineates lesion boundaries with pixel-level precision and, (iii) a severity grading head infers clinically relevant level of lesion depth by reasoning about enamel–dentin–pulp relations and amplitude of radiographic attenuation. Joint optimization across all tasks allows C³-DRIVE Net to reduce errors propagated through the cascaded pipeline while maintaining consistency between disease detection, segmentation, and severity estimation levels in order to improve diagnostic reliability and clinical interpretability. ​ Figure 1. segments.text: ​ Figure 3: Workflow of the C³-DRIVE Net Framework for Unified Dental Caries Analysis The end-to-end workflow of C³-DRIVE Net is illustrated in Figure 3. The system integrates tooth-aware anatomical decomposition, radiographic gradient disruption modeling and multi-task learning. In this integrated design, the model is capable of conducting caries detection, lesion segmentation and clinically-meaningful severity grading all together on dental X-ray images for accurate and interpretable diagnosis. IV Experimental Setup​ 4.1 Dataset Description​ The experiments were done with the open data Kaggle dataset “A Collection of Dental X-ray Images for Analysis” available at:https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/kvipularya/a-collection-of-dental-x-ray-images-fo r-analysis. The dataset consists of nearly 2500 dental radiographic images, such as bitewing, panoramic and periapical X-rays reflected from a variety of imaging landscapes. The images possess differing contrast, tooth shapes, and radiographic noise which render the dataset a good candidate for robust dental caries analysis methodologies. All images are in gray-scale and with varying resolution from 512×512 to 1024×1024 pixels.
segments.label: human

segments.text: Following the elimination of low quality and duplicated images, 2,400 X-rays were used for the experiments. We once split the database through a patient-independent random separation as follows: ●​ Training set: 1,680 images (70%) ●​ Validation set: 360 images (15%) ●​ Testing set: 360 images (15%) This division enables fair testing and enough data to train stabilised hyperparameters. 4.2 Annotation Protocol and Clinical Realism As there is no lesion-level annotated ground truth in the dataset, these were manually annotated for outside of the study. Dental caries area was annotated with pixel-wise annotation to produce the segmentation masks and at tooth level for detection labels. The lesions were graded according to depth taking into account enamel involvement, dentinal extension, and distance from the pulp chamber using radiographically-acceptant clinical interpretation concepts. For increased label reliability, unclear cases were carefully checked and decisions made in the group to make the labels reflect real clinical diagnostic reasoning rather than visual features only. 4.3 Training Details All experiments were conducted with the PyTorch library. Input images were resized to 512×512 and normalized with z-score normalization. Data augmentation such as horizontal flipping, rotation and intensity scaling have been used when training the network to promote robust model. The model was trained with Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 1×10⁻⁴, batch size = 8 and for a maximum of 100 epochs. We used early stopping through validation loss to avoid overfitting. The weights of the multi-task loss were empirically modified for balancing detection, segmentation, and severity grading tasks. 4.4 Baseline Models We compare C³-DRIVE Net with commonly used deep learning baselines in dental caries analysis to verify its performance: ●​ ResNet-50 for image-level caries detection ●​ YOLOv5 for object-based lesion localization ●​ U-Net for pixel-wise caries segmentation ●​ Two-stage CNN systems, which first detect and then classify the severity The datasets splits, preprocessing and augmentation were performed with all the other baselines models as well in order to provide fair comparison 4.5 Evaluation Metrics

The C³-DRIVE Net outperforms conventional models with moderate to strong performance in each task, and consistently obtains the highest scores across all of the metrics: a detection accuracy 97.8%, a segmentation Dice’s coefficient 91.2%, a severity grading accuracy 95.6% and an early stage caries sensitivity of 87%. The results provide evidence in support of the unified, context-aware, and clinically-driven design of C³-DRIVE Net which effectively alleviates the issues encountered by single-task and cascaded frameworks, resulting in a robust and clinically applicable solution for automated dental radiographic diagnosis. 5.1 Ablation study​ To investigate the role of each part in C³-DRIVE Net, an ablation study was performed by adding the main components one by one with other training settings fixed. Indeed, the baseline model featured a common encoder with multiple task heads and did not consider any anatomy or clinical context. With tooth-aware anatomical decomposition, both caries detection and lesion segmentation were also improved as the model can even reason at the level of a tooth. Incorporating radiographic gradient disruption modeling further increased the ability to detect subtle intensity changes, thereby enhancing early caries detection. The most accurate model included a clinically based severity grading, since this was the only one to explicitly reflect the sequence of enamel, dentin and pulp. And the model with all modules delivered an even more balanced and consistent performance that demonstrated each module contributed complementary value.

The base multi-task encoder performed reasonably well; however, it was not very effective in identifying early caries diagnosis. Tooth-aware anatomical decomposition enhanced the structural localization and segmentation performance, while radiographic gradient disruption modeling increased sensitivity to subtle lesion patterns. The entire model containing clinical adjusted severity grading received the best overall scores in all assessment measures. These findings validate that the integrated approach increases detection performance, segmentation performance, and early lesion recognition while reinforcing one another. 5.2 Discussion​ In summary, the experimental results show that C³-DRIVE Net is a promising alternative to conventional deep learning models of DC analyses by collaboratively doing detection, segmentation, and severity grading in one go. The performance of the model reached a detection accuracy of 97.8%, a segmentation Dice score of 91.2% and severity grading accuracy rating of 95.6%. The substantial 22% enhancement in performance of early caries detection is particularly noteworthy with reference to the efficiency considering that modeling radiographic intensity disruptions plays a critical role in detecting subtle enamel demineralization. The ablation study validates that each component in the architecture contributes to superior performance not only on accuracy, but also interpretability and clinical relevance, which demonstrates C³-DRIVE Net is well-suited for real-world chairside diagnostic support. 5.3 Limitations and Future Work While C³-DRIVE Net showed promising performance, this study is constrained by the use of only one open dataset, a representative selection of data not necessarily capturing all heterogeneity observed in multi-center clinical context. The grading of severity is based on a radiographic interpretation only, and does not include clinically supportive evidence or longitudinal follow-up records. Future studies will aim to validate this framework on larger and multi-institutional datasets as well as extend it to 3D modalities including CBCT. In

segments.text: addition, the integration of temporal analysis as well as clinician-in-the-loop feedback systems may improve robustness and clinical applicability. ​ VI Conclusion​ A fully automatic and context-aware unified deep learning framework, named C³-DRIVE Net was introduced in this paper for detection, segmentation and severity grading of dental caries from radiographs on clinical ground. Through combining tooth-sensitive anatomical decomposition, radiographic gradient disturbance modeling, and multi-task learning in a unified deep network, the proposed approach could alleviate the constraints of traditional single-task and cascaded DL models. Experimental results indicate that C³-DRIVE Net is a robust and well-performing model in all diagnostic tasks with 97.8% detection accuracy, 91.2% Dice coefficient, and 95.6% accuracy of severity grading for detection, segmentation, severity grading respectively on independent test dataset. Of significance, the framework achieves 87% sensitivity for detecting early stage caries, which is a WHO Special Service target; this improves prior deep learning-based baselines by 22%. The ablation study verifies that each architectural module has a synergistic effect on the overall performance improvement. The all-in-one framework minimizes error propagation with clinically meaningful anatomically and depth aware severity reasoning. These results emphasize the potential for C³-DRIVE Net-based system to be utilised as an effective chairside diagnostic aid, which could enable early interventions, facilitate objective severity scoring and enhance clinical decision-making in a dental setting.
